decisions.quote: The results for number-based matches partially held when the total match score was used as the dependent variable (Figure 2b). Consistent with the best match score analyses, the significant main effect of Salience held, F(1, 89) = 10.16, p = .002, !! " = .102, with adults selecting number-based matches more frequently when alternative choices were of low salience (M = 4.16, SD = 3.00) compared to high salience (M = 3.38, SD = 3.29). The significant main effect of Order also held, F(1, 89) = 5.08, p = .027, !! " = .054, with adults making number- based matches more frequently when low salience trials came first (M = 4.49, SD = 3.17) compared to when high salience trials came first (M = 3.14, SD = 3.04). However, unlike this sample’s best match score or the total match scores we reported earlier (Chan & Mazzocco, 2017), there was no significant Salience × Order interaction on total match scores, p = .567, !! " = .004.
decisions.reason: While both studies replicate the main effect of salience on attention to numerosity, the primary replication analyses also explicitly test order effects and Salience × Order interactions across best-match and total-match scores and directly contrast several results with Chan & Mazzocco (2017) (e.g., 'unlike this sample’s best match score or the total match scores we reported earlier (Chan & Mazzocco, 2017), there was no significant Salience × Order interaction on total match scores', as well as differing order and interaction results for orientation and best-match scores, and the General Discussion summary that 'we replicated most of our earlier findings'). Under the codebook, confirming a specific main effect does not override explicit author-stated contrasts on tested replication comparisons, making the outcome 'mixed'.
